title: Formation of charge-polarized regions at dual single-atom sites for C-H bond activation in methane

paper_content.abstract: Direct conversion of CH4 into liquid oxygenates under mild conditions is of great significance but remains challenging due to the high dissociation energy of inert C-H bond. Here we report the fabrication of a dual atomic Fe and Pd catalyst with periodic macroporous structure (Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC) toward the direct CH4 conversion at room temperature. Mechanism studies reveal that a charge polarization region (Oδ−-Fe-Pdδ+) is formed in-situ on Fe-Pd atomic sites upon oxidant activation, wherein the electron-rich Oδ− and electron-deficient Pdδ+ regions can respectively capture the Hδ+ and CH3δ− in CH4 and lead to the activation of C-H bond. As a result, Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC demonstrates attractive photothermal catalytic performance toward the selective oxidation of CH4 under Xe lamp irradiation, achieving the productivities of C1 oxygenates as high as 0.754 mmol h−1 and 0.035 mmol h−1 when using H2O2 or O2 as the oxidant, respectively.
paper_content.introduction:
Methane (CH4), the primary constituent of natural gas, is one of the most promising C1 building blocks for the synthesis of high-value fuels and chemicals due to its high reserves and relatively low price1,2. Conventionally, the conversion of CH4 to value-added products mainly involves the strongly endothermic steam reforming (CH4 + H2O → 3H2 + CO, ΔH = +206 kJ mol−1) and the subsequent Fischer-Tropsch synthesis or methanol (CH3OH) synthesis process3,4. However, a high temperature (700–1000 °C) is required to destroy the non-polar tetrahedral structure of CH4 with very high dissociation energy of C–H bond (439.3 kJ mol−1). This high energy input will inevitably lead to the formation of more thermodynamically stable over-oxidation products (i.e., CO2) and coke5. In this case, direct conversion of CH4 into liquid oxygenates at low temperatures should be a promising way to substitute the energy-intensive protocols, which, however, remains an enormous challenge.

In nature, methane monooxygenase (MMO) and cytochrome P450 containing single- or dual-metal centers can directly transform CH4 to oxygenates under mild conditions6,7. Inspired by the natural enzyme catalysis, bioinspired heterogeneous catalysts with isolated metal sites have been developed in recent years, which have demonstrated attractive activity toward CH4 conversion at low temperatures (<100 °C) with the assistance of oxidants (e.g., H2O2, O2). Among these biomimetic active sites, d-block element-isolated centers have drawn enormous attention due to the easy orbital hybridization between their inherent d-orbitals (dz2, dxz and dyz orbitals) and the p/s orbitals of CH4 8–12.

Engineering active centers with a high affinity and bond cleavage capability toward the first C–H bond in CH4 is a promising avenue to obtain a high yield of value-added products. Accordingly, the covalent C–H (four covalent bonds) is composed of 74% ground state and 26% ionic resonance structures13,14. During the CH4 activation process, electrons can migrate between the d orbital of catalyst and the σ orbital of a C–H bond, leading to the cleavage of C–H bond. Alternatively, C–H bond can also be activated in the form of electrostatic CH3δ−-Hδ+ polarization by a localized electrostatic field on catalyst surface5,15,16. For example, Zheng et al. found that the transfer of electrons from ZnO to Fe2O3 can induce the charge accumulation on Fe sites, thus reducing the CH4 adsorption energy and facilitating the activation of C–H bond17. In this regard, the activation of C–H bonds in CH4 is highly sensitive to the electronic status of metal centers. Enlightened by these premises, we envisage that a precise design of the electronic configuration of the catalyst surface would provide opportunities in manipulating the cleavage behavior toward C–H bonds to boost the selective conversion of CH4 under mild conditions.

Here, we address the challenge of C–H bond activation in CH4 by introducing a strategy based on the in-situ construction of charge-polarized regions on asymmetric diatomic active sites via oxidant modification. As a proof of concept, we design and fabricate atomically dispersed Fe and Pd on ordered macroporous nitrogen-doped carbon (denoted as Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC) using an encapsulation-pyrolysis strategy. Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits high photothermal catalytic performance toward the selective oxidation of CH4 when using H2O2 or O2 as the oxidant. Ab-initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations and in-depth in-situ investigations manifest that the oxidant prefers to be activated on Fe site to an axial *O during the photothermal catalytic process, forming a charge polarization region on Oδ−-Fe-Pdδ+. Within this region, the electron-rich Oδ− region captures Hδ+ in CH4, initiating electron transfer that leads to C–H bond cleavage. The electron-deficient Pdδ+ sites stabilize the resulting CH3 species, achieving the complete activation of the CH4 molecule.
paper_content.results:
Synthesis and characterization of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC
The synthetic route of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC is briefly illustrated in Fig. 1a. In brief, the ordered polystyrene spheres (PS) arrays were first prepared by assembling the monodisperse PS (270 nm in diameter) (Supplementary Fig. 1)18. Subsequently, ZIF-8 precursors (i.e., Zn2+ and 2-methylimidazole), Fe3+ and Pd(acac)2 were filled in the PS arrays to form the precursors@PS, which was then immersed in a mixture of CH3OH/NH3·H2O to induce the growth of ZIF-8 single crystals within the template (denoted as FePd-ZIF@PS) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The FePd-ZIF@PS was subjected to pyrolysis in Ar atmosphere to carbonize the ZIF and simultaneously remove the PS template (decomposition temperature of ca. 400 °C) and Zn species (vaporization temperature of ca. 900 °C), leaving Fe and Pd sites embedded in the ordered macroporous N-doped carbon matrix19,20.

No diffraction peaks attributed to ZIF-8 are observed in the powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC (Supplementary Fig. 3). In addition, the Raman spectrum of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits the distinct D band (ca. 1350 cm−1) and G band (ca. 1590 cm−1) of graphitized carbon, reflecting the complete carbonization of ZIF (Supplementary Fig. 4). Notably, the ID/IG ratio of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC is slightly greater than that of OMNC, suggesting that the introduction of metal species can induce the formation of defects in the carbon skeleton (Supplementary Table 1). The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image unveils the monodispersed tetrakaidekahedral particles of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC with eight (111) facets and six (100) facets (Fig. 1b–d). The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and the high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images reveal the oriented arrangement of 3D-ordered macropores interconnected by the mesoporous channels in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 5). The hierarchically porous structure of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC was further confirmed by the N2 sorption isotherm, which shows a steep increase at relatively low pressures (P/P0 < 0.05) and an obvious hysteresis loop (Fig. 1f). For comparison, isolated Fe and Pd sites embedded in the carriers of mesoporous N-doped carbon matrix (Fe-Pd1-Pd1 MeNC) and disordered macroporous N-doped carbon matrix (Fe-Pd1-Pd1 DOMNC) were designed and prepared in the absence of PS or using the discrete PS as the template, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 6, 7). Significantly, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC (670.18 m2/g) is larger than that of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 MeNC (232.08 m2/g) and Fe-Pd1-Pd1 DOMNC (269.26 m2/g), confirming the virtue of ordered hierarchically porous structure (Supplementary Fig. 8). Considering that CH4 conversion reaction occurs on the surface of catalyst, such periodic porous structure and large BET surface area of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC should be conducive to improving the accessibility of active sites.

Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping images reveal the homogeneous dispersions of Fe and Pd elements over the ordered macroporous framework (Fig. 1g, h). No obvious nanoparticles are observed in the high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC (Supplementary Fig. 9). Additionally, no characteristic reflections indexed to Fe or Pd metallic phases are detected by XRD, ruling out the presence of large-sized metal species (Supplementary Fig. 3). Aberration-corrected high angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) image clearly reveals the atomic dispersion of Fe and Pd on the NC skeleton, in which the distance of the atomic pairs is estimated to be ca. 0.35 nm (Fig. 1i, j). The contents of Fe and Pd in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC are measured to be 0.58 and 0.35 wt%, respectively by the inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (Supplementary Table 2).

To clarify the coordination environments of Fe and Pd sites in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC, X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analysis were performed. As shown in Fig. 2a, b, the near-edge absorption energy positions of Fe K-edge and Pd K-edge are located between those of Fe foil and Fe2O3 and those of Pd foil and PdO, respectively, suggesting that both Fe and Pd centers are in oxidized states. The positively charged centers of Fe and Pd can also be discerned by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Supplementary Fig. 10). The Fe K-edge EXAFS spectrum of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits a main peak located at 1.51 Å that is similar to that of FePc, corresponding to the Fe-N scattering path. No Fe-Fe scattering peaks of Fe foil (i.e., 2.17 Å), Fe2O3 (i.e., 2.67 Å) or Fe3O4 (i.e., 2.58 Å) are detected (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 11a). In addition, the k3χ(k) oscillation curve of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC differs from that of Fe foil and Fe2O3, ruling out the presence of metallic Fe or Fe oxide nanoparticles (Supplementary Fig. 11b). In the case of the Pd K-edge FT-EXAFS, a dominant peak at 1.5 Å is observed, corresponding to the Pd-N scattering path21. No Pd-Pd scattering peaks of Pd foil (i.e., 2.50 Å) or PdO (i.e., 2.93 Å) are detected (Fig. 2d). The metal-N paths in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC were also confirmed by the wavelet transform (WT)-EXAFS. As shown in Fig. 2g and supplementary Fig. 12, the WT contour plots of Fe K-edge and Pd K-edge display the intensity maxima at ca. 4 and 6 Å−1, corresponding to the Fe-N and Pd-N scatterings, respectively. Moreover, no Fe-Pd signal is observed in the FT-EXAFS and WT-EXAFS spectra, ruling out the presence of Fe-Pd coordination in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC. According to the well-matched EXAFS fitting, the coordination numbers of Fe-N and Pd-N in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC are calculated to be ca. 4 and 3, respectively. Thus, a probable neighboring Fe-N4C and Pd-N3C structure is proposed (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Supplementary Tables 3, 4).

Accordingly, we thermodynamically and kinetically predicted four possible structures of Fe-Pd-NxCy namely Fe-Pd-N6C1, Fe-Pd-N7C1-I, Fe-Pd-N7C1-II and Fe-Pd-N6C1-III in order to accurately characterize the Fe-Pd coordination (Supplementary Fig. 14). Among these structures, Fe-Pd-N6C1 exhibits a simulated Fe-Pd distance of 3.5 Å, which is very close to the experimental result (Fig. 1j). In addition, density functional theory (DFT) calculation results show that the Fe-Pd-N6C1 model is the most thermodynamically favorable structure due to its lowest system energy. Ab-initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were then performed for a duration of 10 ps to verify the structural feasibility of Fe-Pd-N6C1 model22,23. As shown in Fig. 2e, Supplementary Movie 1 and Supplementary Data 1, the energy of the proposed structure fluctuates within a constant range during the AIMD simulation even at a high temperature of 875 K. In addition, the radial distribution function (RDF) results reveal that the Fe and Pd atoms are directly bonded to the surrounded N atoms with the average metal-N bond lengths of 1.93 and 2.05 Å, which can be well maintained in the AIMD process, reflecting its structural stability (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 15). Indeed, DFT theoretical calculations indicate that the Fe-Pd-N6C1 model is more favorable for the activation of C–H bond in methane compared to other Fe-Pd models or dual Fe and Pd sites. Therefore, the subsequent calculation of the CH4 oxidation reaction pathway is based on the Fe-Pd-N6C1 structure.

Photocatalytic performance of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC
The selective oxidation of CH4 was performed in an autoclave under the irradiation of Xenon arc lamp using H2O2 as oxidant without external heat (Supplementary Fig. 16). All the possible liquid (e.g., alcohols, hydroperoxide, and organic acids) and gas products (e.g., CO, C2H4, C2H6 and CO2) were quantitatively analyzed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), gas chromatography (GC) and ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer (Supplementary Figs. 17–19). As shown in Supplementary Figs. 20, 21, C1 oxygenates including HCOOH, CH3OH and CH3OOH are detected as the main products, apart from the trace amount of overoxidized products. Notably, the as-prepared Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibit high catalytic performance toward the selective oxidation of CH4, delivering a total C1 oxygenates evolution rate as high as 0.754 mmol h−1 with a selectivity of 100%. The turnover frequency (TOF) is calculated to be 1106.4 h−1, corresponding to 16.2 mol gmetal−1 h−1. The apparent quantum yield (AQY) at 450 nm is estimated to be 3.34%. Notably, the yield of oxygenates achieved in this work is competitive with prior studies (Supplementary Table 5).

For comparison, three control samples namely Fe1 OMNC, Pd1 OMNC and OMNC were synthesized (Supplementary Figs. 22–24). As shown in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 25, Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC reveals a higher evolution rate of total oxygenates than Fe1 OMNC (0.455 mmol h−1), Pd1 OMNC (0.330 mmol h−1) and OMNC (0.138 mmol h−1). Notably, the yield of C1 oxygenates over the physical mixture of Fe1 OMNC and Pd1 OMNC (0.552 mmol h−1) is significantly lower than that over Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC (0.754 mmol h−1) (Supplementary Fig. 26), suggesting that the enhanced catalytic activity of the bimetallic system originates from the synergistic effect between the adjacent Fe and Pd dual-atom sites. In addition, OMNC without metal species displays lower oxygenates evolution rate compared with the atomic metal samples, suggesting that metal species may be the active sites for CH4 conversion and Fe-Pd synergy plays an indispensable role in improving the catalytic activity. Notably, both Fe-Pd1-Pd1 DOMNC with disordered macropores and Fe-Pd1-Pd1 MeNC without macropores show poor catalytic activities with the C1 oxygenates evolution rates of 0.444 and 0.325 mmol h−1, respectively, pointing out the virtue of ordered macroporous structure in realizing the full catalytic potentials of Fe-Pd atomic catalyst (Fig. 3b). The sequential cycling test demonstrates that the catalytic performance of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC can be maintained at a high level with a C1 oxygenated products yield of 0.743 mmol h−1 after eight consecutive cycles (Fig. 3c). Moreover, the SEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX mapping images, XRD pattern and XPS spectra indicate that the morphology and structure of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC remain intact after the catalytic reactions, highlighting its good stability (Supplementary Fig. 27).

Control experiments reveal that the partial pressure of CH4 is conductive to the catalytic performance toward CH4 conversion (Supplementary Fig. 28). In addition, CH4 conversion is terminated in the absence of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC or H2O2, reflecting the essential roles of catalyst and oxidant in CH4 oxidation (Fig. 3d, columns 1–2). The effect of the amounts of H2O2 and catalysts on the catalytic activity was then explored. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 29, increasing the H2O2 content promotes the formation of oxygenated products. However, excessive H2O2 results in decreased oxygenate yields, which may be ascribed to the overoxidation of liquid products24. Moreover, the yields of C1 oxygenated products significantly increase as the dosage of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC changes from 1 to 5 mg. Nevertheless, further increments in catalyst dosage will attenuate the rate of performance enhancement (Supplementary Fig. 30).

No detectable oxygenates are observed when replacing CH4 feedstock gas with Ar, indicating that the oxygenated products are originated from the oxidation of CH4 (Fig. 3d, column 3). The carbon balance of the present photothermal catalytic system is higher than 97%, suggesting that the C1 oxygenated products came from the transformation of CH4 (Supplementary Fig. 31). To confirm the source of the product, we further conducted the 13C isotope labeling experiment using 13CH4 as the feedstock. As shown in Fig. 3e, the 13C NMR spectra reveal that the featured peaks match well with the 13C-labeled formic acid (H13COOH), methyl hydroperoxide (13CH3OOH), and methanol (13CH3OH), indicating that the C1 oxygenated products came from the oxidation of 13CH4 rather than from the catalyst itself.

The reaction in the absence of Xe lamp irradiation gave unsatisfactory oxygenate yield of 0.030 mmol h−1, suggesting the essential role of light irradiation (Fig. 3d, column 5). In contrast, the generation rate of C1 oxygenated products increases gradually with an increase in the light intensity (Supplementary Fig. 32). Interestingly, further increasing the light intensity leads to an increase in the selectivity of CH3OH and a decrease in CH3OOH yield, indicating that intense light irradiation may promote the conversion process of CH3OOH to CH3OH25,26.

We thus investigated the optical properties of the catalysts by diffuse reflection spectrometer. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 33, Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits intensive light absorption across the UV-Vis-IR region. In addition, the infrared thermal images demonstrate that the temperature of the surface of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC immediately raises from room temperature to 195.9 °C upon the irradiation of Xe light, implying its good photothermal conversion property (insert of Supplementary Fig. 33). We thus monitored the temperature variation of the homogeneous reaction solution during the catalytic process (Supplementary Figs. 34, 35). The results show that the temperature of the reaction solution in the presence of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC rapidly increases from room temperature to a maximum temperature of 62.8 °C following the irradiation of Xe lamp, which is significantly higher than that without catalyst (48.2 °C).

To further identify the role of light irradiation, the oxidation of CH4 was performed under the photocatalytic (with 25 °C circulating water) and thermal catalytic conditions (only electric heating). Interestingly, both the solely photocatalytic and thermal catalytic systems display lower oxygenated products yields of 0.286 and 0.233 mmol h−1, respectively compared with the photothermal catalytic system (Fig. 3d, columns 6–7). We further performed the thermal catalytic CH4 oxidation experiments at different temperatures under dark condition. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 36, the generation rate of C1 oxygenates increases gradually from 0.030 to 0.233 mmol h−1 when increasing the temperature from 25 to 63 °C. However, kinetic analysis demonstrates that the apparent activation energy for CH4 oxidation under photothermal condition (27.73 KJ mol−1) is significantly lower than that under purely thermal condition (48.84 KJ mol−1) (Fig. 3f). These results indicate that the oxidation of CH4 is facilitated by photothermal synergy, rather than by simple light-induced thermal catalysis alone.

To further distinguish between purely thermal and photo-assisted thermal process, we measured the reaction rate at a constant temperature (i.e., 63 °C) while varying the light intensity. As shown in Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. 37, the yield of C1 oxygenates in Fe‑Pd1-Pd1 OMNC system increases significantly from 0.416 to 0.798 mmol h−1 as the light intensity increases from 100 to 600 mW cm−2, while the temperature is maintained at 63 °C by external heating. Combined with the results of a series of controlled experiments (Fig. 3f, g, Supplementary Figs. 35–40 and Supplementary Table 7), it can be fully demonstrated that light primarily generates photoexcited electrons and directly participates in the catalytic steps, while the photo-driven heat accelerates the overall reaction kinetics.

In fact, the catalytic performance of Fe‑Pd1-Pd1 OMNC photothermal system decreases by 50.36% after adding an electron scavenger (i.e., AgNO3) (Supplementary Fig. 39a)27. In addition, an obvious photocurrent signal is observed in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC upon light irradiation, confirming the generation of excited electrons. Significantly, the photocurrent increases while the electron transfer resistance of Fe‑Pd1-Pd1 OMNC decreases as the solution temperature rises from 25 to 63 °C (Supplementary Figs. 39b, c, 40 and Supplementary Table 7). These results unambiguously demonstrate that photo-induced heat in Fe‑Pd1-Pd1 OMNC plays an indispensable role in promoting the generation and lowering the migration resistance of photoexcited electrons. In addition, Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits a higher current density and smaller semicircle diameter in electrochemical impedance spectroscopy than OMNC, suggesting that the presence of dual Fe-Pd metals sites can promote the formation of photo-induced electron (Supplementary Figs. 41, 42).

In-situ irradiated XPS was then carried out to explore the charge transfer within Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 43, both the high-resolution Fe 2p and Pd 3d XPS spectra display the distinct positive shifts upon light irradiation, while the N 1s spectrum exhibits a negative shift. Such shifts in binding energy under light irradiation confirm the migration of photo-induced electrons between N and metal sites. The above results unambiguously reveal that heat and photo-induced electrons generated by Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC under light irradiation would jointly participate in the oxidation of CH4, instead of undergoing a simple photo-derived thermal catalysis (Supplementary Fig. 44). On the one hand, the formed photoexcited charge carriers and thermal energy are able to directly participate the activation of CH4. On the other hand, the photo-induced heat can also promote the generation and migration dynamics of photoexcited charge carriers, thereby enhancing the efficiency of electron-involved activation process.

We also conducted the photothermal catalytic CH4 oxidation over Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC by using both O2 and H2O2 as the oxidants. As shown in Fig. 3h, the introduction of O2 significantly increased the total C1 oxygenates evolution rate from 0.754 to 1.480 mmol h−1. Considering the high cost and safety issues of hydrogen peroxide during the catalytic process, we subsequently employed sole O2 as the oxidant for the selective oxidation of CH4. Satisfyingly, the as-prepared Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC demonstrates high catalytic performance in the selective oxidation of CH4 with a methanol production rate of 0.035 mmol h−1 (Supplementary Fig. 45). Further, we pre-treated the Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC with H2O2 at room temperature (denoted as O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC) and performed the photothermal catalytic CH4 oxidation under O2 to avoid the formation of deep-oxidized product (i.e., HCOOH)28. Unexpectedly, the as-prepared O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibit high total C1 oxygenates evolution rate of 0.996 mmol h−1 with a methanol yield of 0.787 mmol h−1, highlighting the structural virtue of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC in CH4 oxidation (Fig. 3i). Notably, the oxygenate yield in this work demonstrates competitiveness compared to previously reported CH4 conversion catalysts under comparable conditions (Supplementary Table 6).

To gain insights into the catalytic mechanism of CH4 conversion, in-situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra with the spin-electron trap (i.e., 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide, DMPO) were conducted to monitor the formed free radicals29,30. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 46, DMPO-OOH and DMPO-OH were detected in the presence of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC under irradiation, suggesting that •OOH and •OH radicals were formed during the photothermal catalytic process. Notably, a new sextet signal emerges after the introduction of CH4 in the reaction solution (Fig. 4a), which could be assigned to the •CH3 radical31. These results manifest that the •OOH and •OH radicals generated from H2O2 decomposition are able to attack CH4 to form the •CH3 radical under the irradiation of Xe lamp.

In-situ diffuse Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was employed to probe the reaction intermediates on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC during the photothermal CH4 conversion process. As shown in Fig. 4b, c, two peaks appear at 881 and 1643 cm−1 as the reaction proceeds, corresponding to the *OOH and *OH species, respectively32. Additional peak responsible for methyl (*CH3) emerges at 1354, 1455 and 1410 cm−1, reflecting the activation of C–H bond in CH4 to give rise of *CH3 on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC33,34. It is noted that two adsorption bands belonged to *O=COOH and *CH3O appear at 1340 and 2820 cm−1, suggesting the formation of HCOOH and CH3OH in the reaction system35. Accordingly, a possible pathway for the photothermal conversion of CH4 over Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC is deduced as follow: *CH4 → *CH3 → *CH3OH/*CH3OOH/*HCOOH.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were intervened to explore the catalytic mechanism for the selective oxidation of CH4 on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC. Three calculation models, i.e., Fe single-atom site (Fe-N4C3), Pd single-atom site (Pd-N4C3), and Fe-Pd dual-single-atomic sites (Fe-Pd-N6C1), were constructed based on the results of EXAFS (Supplementary Figs. 14, 47, Supplementary Data 1). We studied the dissociation behavior of H2O2 on catalyst surface. It is observed in Supplementary Fig. 48 that H2O2 can be readily adsorbed on the metal atomic sites and activated into •OH or •OOH species. Significantly, H2O2 prefers to be activated on the Fe site in Fe-Pd-N6C1 with a lower energy barrier compared with that on Fe-N4C3 and Pd-N4C3, signifying the synergistic effect of Fe-Pd diatomic sites on H2O2 activation. Interestingly, we found that the activation of O2 molecule on Fe-Pd diatomic center is consistent with the activation process of H2O2. As observed in Supplementary Fig. 49, O2 can be easily captured by the Fe site in Fe-Pd-N6C1 and activated into *OOH with a gibbs free energy difference of as small as 0.48 eV. Subsequently, the formed *OOH can be further activated into *O species to formed the O-Fe-Pd structure.

AIMD simulations were then conducted to gain insight into the activation behavior of H2O2 on Fe-Pd-N6C1. Interestingly, the results of AIMD simulations demonstrate that the active O species can be formed on the Fe site in Fe-Pd-N6C1 via a hydrogen transfer process between two OH* groups during the H2O2 activation process (Supplementary Fig. 50, Supplementary Movie 2 and Supplementary Data 1). The formed in-situ axially coordinated O species on Fe site is able to stabilize the Fe-Pd-N6C1 structure with a total energy decrease of 2.50 eV, which is well in line with previous works (Supplementary Fig. 51)36,37. Actually, the formation of O species on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC has been confirmed by XPS spectra, which show that the proportion of Fe–O bond (529.5 eV) in O 1s increases significantly after the treatment of H2O2 (Supplementary Fig. 52).

Subsequently, we proposed the plausible reaction pathways of CH4 conversion to C1 oxygenates on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC and further gained in-depth insight into these steps via DFT calculations, in which Fe-Pd-N6C1 structure was selected as the models of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC (Supplementary Fig. 53a). As shown in the energy profile diagrams (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Figs. 53, 54), the dissociation of C–H bond on Fe-Pd-N6C1 is endothermic (ΔG = 1.44 eV), suggesting the C–H bond activation process should be the rate-limiting step in CH4 conversion. The generated methyl species after the activation of C–H bond can combine with •OH and •OOH easily to form the CH3OH, CH3OOH, and HCOOH products as these steps are exothermic. It is clear that the activation energy required for C–H bond dissociation on the pristine Fe-Pd-N6C1 is calculated to be 2.72 eV (Supplementary Fig. 55a). In contrast, the activation energy barrier significantly decreases to 1.82 eV upon the implantation of axially coordinated O species on Fe site, pointing out the essential role of O species in CH4 activation (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 55b). In addition, a higher energy barrier of 2.23 eV is required to activate the C–H bond on the single atom Fe site (i.e., Fe-N4C3) in the absence of Pd (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 55c). These results demonstrate that the co-existing dual atomic sites and O species, namely O-Fe-Pd structure is beneficial for the activation of CH4.

To delve into the roles of O-Fe-Pd structure on C–H bond activation, we conducted AIMD simulations to investigate the dynamic adsorption and activation process of CH4. In the case of the pristine Fe-Pd-N6C1, CH4 molecule tends to approach and circle around the Fe site via a weak physical interaction (Supplementary Movie 3 and Supplementary Fig. 56a). During the AIMD simulations, the bond-length of C–H in CH4 molecule keeps stable at ca. 0.13 Å and only 0.003 e− of electron transformation between CH4 and pristine Fe-Pd-N6C1 is observed, revealing its non-activated state (Supplementary Fig. 56b, c and Supplementary Table 8). By contrary, when CH4 approaches the O-Fe-Pd sites formed by O coordination, the H atom in CH4 can be captured by the axial O atom to form a Fe-OH ensemble and the residual CH3 group is stabilized by the Pd site (Fig. 4f, g and Supplementary Movie 4). During the activation process, one of the C–H bond lengths in CH4 molecule dynamically elongates from 0.98 Å to 3.02 Å, suggesting the complete activation of CH4 molecule (Supplementary Fig. 57).

Notably, the C–H activation behavior on O assisted single atomic Fe-N4C3 (i.e., O-Fe site) is similar to that on O-Fe-Pd site except that the residual CH3 group tends to be captured by Fe site (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 55c). In this case, the *H atom and *CH3 on O-Fe site will inevitably undergo a recombination process due to their close distance. Such a reverse activation is also observed by the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculation, which reveals that the reaction barrier for the recombination of *CH3 and *H on O-Fe site (2.09 eV) is significantly lower than that on O-Fe-Pd site (2.23 eV) and even the CH4 activation on O-Fe site (2.23 eV) (Supplementary Fig. 58). The aforementioned results unambiguously confirm the virtue of the as-formed O-Fe-Pd structure in CH4 activation.

To further confirm the activation process of CH4 on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC, time-resolved FTIR spectra over Fe1 OMNC and Pd1 OMNC were performed (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 59). The results show that the intensity of the *CH3 signals on Pd1 OMNC is significantly higher than that on Fe1 OMNC (Fig. 4i). Additionally, the FTIR band of *CH3 on Pd1 OMNC exhibits a blue shift from 1417 to 1435 cm−1 compared with that on Fe1 OMNC (Supplementary Table 9). The intense signals of *CH3 and the blue shift of the FTIR bands indicate a stronger interaction of Pd-CH3 than Fe-CH338. Additionally, the FTIR bands of *CH3 on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC are closer to that on Pd1 OMNC but farther away from that on Fe1 OMNC, suggesting that the generated *CH3 intermediate during the CH4 activation process is more readily captured by Pd sites.

We then performed CH4-temperature programmed desorption (CH4-TPD) measurements to further understand the chemical adsorption behavior of CH4. As shown in Fig. 4j and Supplementary Fig. 60, Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC exhibits a larger desorption quantity and higher desorption temperature (256 °C) of CH4 compared with that of single atom catalysts (i.e., Fe1 OMNC and Pd1 OMNC), suggesting a stronger CH4 adsorption on Fe-Pd diatomic sites. In addition, the CH4 desorption peak over Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC shifts to a higher temperature (265 °C) and becomes more intense when decorated with O species, pointing out the significant role of O-Fe-Pd structure in enhancing the interaction between CH4 and catalyst.

To further disclose the activation mechanism of C–H bond on the O-Fe-Pd structure, we analyzed the local structure of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC. As shown in Supplementary Figs. 61–63, both the single atom models of Fe-N4C3 and Pd-N4C3 display the perfectly symmetrical configurations with metal-N bond in length of 1.88 and 1.94 Å, respectively. Electron localization function (ELF) and charge density difference further illustrate the symmetrical distributions of charge densities for Fe-N4C3 and Pd-N4C3. Upon the construction of Fe-Pd dual-single-atomic structure, the symmetrical metal-N geometry and electronic structures are broken. The unbalanced electron configuration in Fe-Pd-N6C1 may be attributed to the differences in electronegativity between Fe and Pd.

The charge density difference was then calculated to quantify the variation of electronic structure induced by axial O species, where its planar average along the Z-direction is plotted. Clearly, Fig. 5a reveals an obvious electron transfer from metal sites to O with the charge of ca. 0.58 e−. Such a migration of electrons should induce the aggregation of electrons on O site. Thus, a charge polarization region should be formed on the O-Fe-Pd structure with the electron-rich and electron-deficient regions located on O and Pd sites, respectively (i.e., Oδ−-Fe-Pdδ+).

Actually, the variation in the surface charge of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC by O implanting is observed by the Zeta potential test, which shows that the charge is changed from −0.60 to −31.5 mV upon the treatment of H2O2 (Fig. 5b). Moreover, the charge of Fe1 OMNC is reduced significantly by 13 mV upon the treatment of H2O2. In contrast, H2O2 treatment displays negligible alter on the charge of Pd1 OMNC and OMNC (Supplementary Fig. 64). The variation in the surface charge of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC by O implanting is also observed by Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), which show that the surface potential increases significantly upon the treatment of H2O2 (Supplementary Fig. 65). These results suggest that the Fe sites in Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC should be the active centers for H2O2 activation and a electron-rich region (Fe–O) is generated after H2O2 treatment. In addition, the contact potential difference (CPD) increases significantly after Xe lamp irradiation, indicating that the charge polarization within Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC can be strengthen upon illumination (Supplementary Fig. 66).

To gain more insights into the electron transfer mechanism within O-Fe-Pd structure, the partial density of states (PDOS) and projected crystal orbital Hamilton population (pCOHP) calculations were performed. It is clearly that the 3d orbital (dz2) of Fe site exhibits a large extent of overlap with the p orbital of O site, pointing out their strong bonding via d-p interaction (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Figs. 67, 68). Fragment orbital analysis show that the electrons in metal d orbitals are partially transferred to the singly occupied 2p orbitals of O via the dz2-pz interaction (Supplementary Fig. 69). In addition, since the d band center of Fe site in Fe-Pd-N6C1 (−2.41 eV) is more positive than that in Fe-N4C3 (−2.76 eV), the antibonding state of d-p in O-Fe-Pd structure shows less electron occupancy compared with that in O-Fe structure (Supplementary Figs. 70, 71). Thus, the electron transfer between O and dual atomic Fe-Pd-N6C1 should be more frequent and the degree of charge polarization is more distinctly than that between O and single atomic Fe-N4C3, which is confirmed by the charge density difference and Bader charge analysis of O-Fe structure (Supplementary Fig. 72a and Supplementary Table 8)39–41.

The formation of charge polarization region on O-Fe-Pd sites may facilitate the activation process of C–H bond. Thus, the electron transfer behavior during the activation of CH4 on O-Fe-Pd sites was analyzed. According to the Mulliken charge analysis, the C and H atoms in CH4 possess the negative (−1.03 e−) and positive charges (+0.25 e−), respectively, before activation (Supplementary Table 8). During the activation process, the positively charged H atom of CH4 is readily captured by the negatively charged O atom of O-Fe-Pd sites, which is witnessed by charge density difference and spin density distribution analysis (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 72b, c)42. The Bader charge calculation further elucidates that the charge of CH3 fragment far from O atom increases by 0.25 e− (Supplementary Table 8). This formed electron-rich region will induce the CH3δ− fragment to be landed on the electron-deficient region (i.e., Pdδ+ site), thus leading to the hetero-cleavage of C–H bond (CH4 + Fe–Oδ− + Pdδ+ → Fe–Oδ−-Hδ+ + CH3δ−-Pdδ+). Actually, the charge of *CH3 fragment decreases by 0.48 e− when bonding to the Pd site.

Further, quasi in-situ XPS was then performed to monitor the variation of chemical states and surface eletrons during the C–H activation process, where Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC was first treated with H2O2 (i.e., O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC) and then subjected to CH4 and light treatment in an in-situ chamber. As shown in Fig. 5e, the surface OH species (531.5 eV) in the O 1s spectrum increases significantly upon light irradiation under CH4 atmosphere, signifying that the H species in CH4 may combine with the surface O species on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC to form the OH species during the C–H bond activation process43. Moreover, the binding energy of Pd 3d significantly shifts towards lower binding energies by 0.4 eV after CH4 and light treatment, suggesting that Pd sites tend to gain electrons during the CH4 activation process44,45. Considering that negative electron nature of the carbon center in *CH3 (Supplementary Table 10), we speculate that the electrons obtained by the Pd sites during CH4 activation are likely to come from the *CH3 fragment.

Fragment orbital analysis was further conducted to explore the orbital interactions and electron transfer mechanisms in the activation process of CH4 on the Oδ−-Fe-Pdδ+ charge-polarized region (Fig. 5f, g and Supplementary Figs. 73–77). The results show that the constructed Oδ−-Fe-Pdδ+ charge polarization region is able to capture CH4, giving rise to the formation of s-p obital interaction between O and H atoms. This s-p orbital interaction then serves as an electronic transport bridge to inject electrons from electron-rich Oδ− sites into the σ* antibonding orbital of CH4, facilitating the breakage of C–H bond. Meanwhile, the electrons in the remained CH3 fragment transfer to the electron-deficient Pd site via p-d coordination interactions, achieving the complete activation of CH4. Nevertheless, due to the inherent simplifications of DFT, there are limitations in modeling the precise electronic structure and dynamic evolution of the charge-polarized region under actual photothermal conditions.

To prove the feasibility of in-situ formed O-Fe-Pd sites for C–H activation, in-situ EPR and in-situ FTIR have been conducted on a precatalyst O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC with O-Fe-Pd sites to explore the activation of CH4 under H2O2 free conditions. As shown in Fig. 5h, a stable CH3 radical signal is detected over O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC without externally added H2O2. In addition, in-situ FTIR spectra exhibit the distinct FTIR bands of *CH3 and *OH on O/Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC upon CH4 and light treatment, while neglectable signals are observed on the surface of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC without H2O2 treatment (Fig. 5i and Supplementary Figs. 78, 79). These results demonstrate that the in-situ formed O-Fe-Pd sites on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC can drive the activation of C–H bond in CH4 under illumination.

Taken together, our findings clearly illustrate that a charge polarization region is formed on Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC upon the construction of O-Fe-Pd structure, which enables the stabilization of *H and *CH3 fragments and thus promotes the activation of CH4. In addition, the periodic macroporous structure of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC with large external surface area can efficiently improve the accessibility of Fe-Pd dual single-atom sites and enhance the mass transfer efficiency toward substrate and products, which contribute to the high photothermal catalytic efficiency toward CH4 conversion. In addition, the ordered macroporous stucture can also enhance the light absorption due to the slow light effects and the band-stop reflection generated by coherent Bragg diffraction19. Particularly, both the light absorption capability and mass transfer efficiency can be significantly amplified if the macropores are periodically arranged into the three-dimensional ordered array.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
All chemicals were commercially purchased and directly used without purification. The following chemicals were purchased and used without any further treatments: ammonium hydroxide (NH3·H2O, 28–30%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, 99.9%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), potassium persulfate (K2S2O8, 99.5%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), palladium acetylacetonate (C10H14O4Pd, 99.95%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), sodium hydroxide pellets (NaOH, 95%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2∙6H2O, 99%, Shanghai Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 6 wt.% in H2O, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), deuterated water (D2O, 99.9%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.), N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.8%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.) and 2-methylimidazole (2-MeIM, 98%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.).

Catalysts synthesis
Synthesis of 3D-PS template. The uniformly monodisperse colloidal PS spheres with a diameter of ~270 nm were first synthesized via a soap-free method. Typically, a mixture of 500 mL of deionized water, 65 mL of styrene, and 2.5 g of polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was sequentially added to a 1 L round-bottom flask, which was purged with nitrogen for 15 min and stirred mechanically at 75 °C. Subsequently, 50 mL of aqueous solution containing 0.1 g of K2S2O8 was added to initiate the polymerization of styrene. After stirring for 24 h under nitrogen atmosphere, monodispersed PS spheres were obtained. The 3D-PS template was prepared by filtering the as-synthesized monodispersed PS spheres.

Synthesis of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC. 3.0 g of 2-methylimidazole was dissolved in 6.0 mL of methanol to obtain solution A. 3.62 g of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, 300 mg of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, and 20 mg of acetylacetone palladium Pd(acac)2 were dissolved in 14 mL of methanol to obtain solution B. The precursor solution was then obtained via mixing the solutions of A and B. Subsequently, a piece of 3D-PS template was added to the precursor solution and impregnated for 1 h, followed by vacuum treatment for 10 min to make sure that the metal species and organic ligands fill the gaps of template. Following impregnation, the precursor@PS was dried at 50 °C overnight. To crystallize the ZIF-8 phase, the dried precursor@PS was then treated with a CH3OH/NH3·H2O (2:1 v/v) solution under vacuum degassing for 5 min, and aged for 24 h at room temperature. The obtained FePd-ZIF@PS was collected and dried at 50 °C prior to pyrolysis. The pyrolysis was conducted in a tubular furnace under flowing Ar, with the temperature programmed to increase at 5 °C/min to 950 °C and held there for 2 h. After cooling to room temperature, the obtained black power was subjected to acid treatment (0.1 M HCl) to remove the residual Zn species and any impurity. In addition, the 3DOM FePd-ZIF with ordered macroporous structure was prepared via soaking FePd-ZIF@PS in N, N-Dimethylformamide to remove the PS template. The synthetic process of OMNC was similar to that of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC except for the absence of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O and Pd(acac)2. The synthetic process of the Fe-Pd1-Pd1 DOMNC with disordered microporous structure was similar to the synthesis of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC except for using the crushed PS filter cake as the template.

Synthesis of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 MeNC. 3.62 g of Zn(NO3)2·6(H2O), 100 mg of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, and 20 mg of acetylacetone palladium were dissolved in 14 mL of methanol, which was then poured into 6 mL of methanol solution containing 3.0 g of 2-methylimidazole. The mixture was stirred for 5 min and let stand at room temperature for 24 h to obtain FePd-ZIF. A pyrolysis and subsequent acid treatment processes similar to the synthesis of Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC were adopted to transfer FePd-ZIF into Fe-Pd1-Pd1 MeNC.

Material characterizations
The morphology observations were conducted on a scanning electron microscopy (SEM, HITACHI SU8220) and a transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEOL, JEM 2100F) equipped with an EDX analyzer (Bruker Xflash 5030T). A FEI Titan Themsis Z high-resolution transmission electron microscope with voltage of 300 kV was utilized to obtain the spherical aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-HAADF-STEM) images. A Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer was used to characterize the crystal structures. A Thermo Scientific NEXSA X-ray photoelectron spectrometer was applied to determined the chemical states of catalysts, where where C 1s peak (284.8 eV) was selected as the ref. 46. Raman spectra were recorded on a Raman spectrometer (HORIBA Jobin Yvon). The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas and porosity were analyzed on an automatic rapid comparison surface and porosity analyzer (Micromeritics, ASAP 2460). The 3D structural model of catalysts in Fig. 1a was created by Blender 5.0, a software package released under the GNU General Public License that grants users full free usage rights (https://www.blender.org/).

X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements, encompassing both XANES and EXAFS, were carried out at the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS). A Si (111) double-crystal monochromator was used to monochromatize the white light. Spectra for Fe and Pd were calibrated against foil and oxide standards (Fe, FeO, Fe2O3, Pd, PdO). All measurements were performed with the storage ring at 2.5 GeV and an electron current maintained below 200 mA. The collected EXAFS data were analyzed via the ATHENA module47.

In-situ Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) tests were conducted on a Thermo Fisher iS50 with a KBr plate as the infrared window, in which CH4 bubbled with H2O2 aqueous solution was adopted as the carrier gas. A 300 W xenon lamp was used as the light source. Free radical capture experiment on electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). 5 mg of sample was dispersed in 4.5 mL water or methanol containing 0.5 mL DMPO solution (1 M). Then, an appropriate amount of solution was taken and loaded into an EPR test tube and purged with CH4 or Ar gas for 5 min before adding 0.5 mL of 30% hydrogen peroxide. EPR spectra were recorded after illumination for 0 minutes (i.e., in the dark), 5 min, and 10 min with a 300 W xenon lamp. The Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) analyses were performed using an atomic force microscope (AFM, Bruker Dimension Icon). The Zeta potential information was obtained using a Malvern Zetasizer Nano series. The contents of Fe and Pd in different catalysts were determined by an inductively coupled plasma atomic emissions spectroscopy (ICP-OES) of PerkinElmer 7300DV instrument.

Photothermal catalytic selective oxidation of CH4
The photothermal catalytic oxidation of methane was conducted in a 230 mL batch reactor equipped with a quartz window to allow light exposure. Typically, 5 mg of catalyst, 5 mL of water and a certain amount of H2O2 or O2 (0.2 MPa) were added to the reactor vessel. The reactor was purged with CH4 multiple times to remove air, and then pressurized with Ar or CH4 (purity of 99.9995%) to reach 2 MPa. A 300 W xenon lamp (CEL-HXF300-T3) was used as the light source and no external heat source was applied. The light intensity of Xenon lamp was measured by automatic strong light power meter (CEL-NP2000-2A, Beijing China Education Au-light Co., Ltd.). Throughout the reaction, the system was stirred at 800 rpm. After reaction, the reactor was cooled to room temperature in an ice bath, and the liquid and gas phase products were gathered. Gas products were analyzed by a gas chromatography (GC) equipped with FID and TCD detectors, while liquid products were analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR, JEOL) with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as the internal standard, respectively. HCHO was determined via the colorimetric method using a U-T3C type ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer. In detail, a 0.25% (v/v) acetylacetone solution was first prepared by mixing 20 g of ammonium acetate, 6 mL of acetic acid, and 0.5 mL of acetylacetone in 100 mL of distilled water. Subsequently, 1.5 mL of the solution was mixed with 1.0 mL of as-prepared acetylacetone solution. The HCHO content was then determined by measuring the absorbance at 413 nm. The experimental data variability for the activity tests was <±5%.

Photoelectrochemical measurement
Electrochemical tests were conducted on a Chenhua CHI760E electrochemical workstation configured with a standard three-electrode system. Fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass slides served as the substrates for photoelectrodes48. A catalyst ink was prepared by mixing 10 mg of the as-prepared samples with of 200 μL ethanol, 800 μL deionized water, and 10 μL Nafion (5 wt.%). This ink was then uniformly coated onto the conductive side of the FTO substrate. The prepared electrode, Pt wire, and Ag/AgCl electrode were used as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. Na2SO4 aqueous solution (0.5 M, PH=7±0.1) was employed as the electrolyte. The pH value of the electrolyte was measured using a pH meter (PHS-3E, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd.). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured with the frequency range of 100,000–0.1 Hz at different conditions. Zview software was used to fit the Nyquist plots to model the process of electrode-electrolyte interface. The data collected by EIS were fitted by an appropriate equivalent circuit, and the values of the parameters were changed until the mathematical function matched the experimental data. All electrochemical tests were conducted in the absence of iR compensation. The applied potential was corrected by converted to the RHE using the equation:
ERHE = E vs:Ag=AgCl + 0:0591 × pH + E0(Ag=AgCl) (1)

The calculation formulas for product yield (mmol·h−1), and selectivity of C1 oxygenated compounds are as follows:
Product yield = n(total oxidation products) / h (2)
C1 oxygenated compounds selectivity (%) = n(C1 oxygenated compounds) / n(total oxidation products) * 100% (3)

In the equation, n(total oxidation products) is the total molecular mole of CH4 oxidation products, n(C1 oxygenated compounds) is the molecular mole of C1 oxygenated compounds. The experimental data variability for the activity tests was <±5%.

The apparent turnover frequency (TOF) of C1 formation was calculated according to:
TOF(h−1) = The mole of C1 (mol) / (The moles of supported metal (mol) × unit time (h)) (4)

In the equation, the mole of C1 is the molecular mole of C1 oxygenated compounds, the moles of supported metal are the sum of the moles of Fe and Pd. The experimental data variability for the activity tests was <±5%.

The apparent Quantum Yield (AQY) of the photothermal catalytic system was measured under the illumination of 100 W LED light (450 nm) at 63 °C, which can be calculated by the following formula:
AQY = Ne × 100% = (v × NA × K × (h × c) / λ) / (I × A × λ) × 100% = 3:34% (5)

where v(HCOOH, CH3OH, CH3OOH) = 3.93889×10−8 mol s−1, 9.99861×10−9 mol s−1, 1.28375×10−7 mol s−1; K(HCOOH, CH3OH, CH3OOH) = 4, 2, 6; NA = 6.022×1023 mol−1; T = 2 h, A = 12.56 cm2; λ = 450 nm, I = 600×10−3 W m−2, h = 6.62×10−34 J s−1, c = 3.0×108 m s−1. For Fe-Pd1-Pd1 OMNC: AQY% = [(4×3.93889×10−8 + 2×9.99861×10−9 + 6×1.28375×10−7)×6.022×1023]×(6.62×10−34×3.0×108) / (600×10−3×12.566×450×10−9) = 3.3410%.

The conversion of CH4 was determined by using Argon as the internal standard, which can be calculated by the following formula:
Con(CH4%) = (n0(CH4) - nt(CH4)) / n0(CH4) × 100% (6)

where n(CH4) and n0(CH4) represent the moles of CH4 after and before the reaction, respectively.

The carbon balance (%) in the photothermal catalytic system can be calculated by the following formula:
carbon balance (%) = n(C1) / n0(CH4) × 100% (7)

where n(C1) and n0(CH4) represent the moles of products and reactant gas, respectively.

Computational details for calculations
The details of DFT calculations. The DFT calculations were performed by Vienna Abinitio Simulation Package (VASP) using the projector augmented wave (PAW) method49,50. The valence electron configurations applied in this work were 2s22p2 (C), 2s22p3 (N), 2s22p4 (O), and 4s² 3d6 (Fe), 4d10 (Pd), respectively. Planar wave cut-off energy (ENCUT) was set to 400 Ev51. A 4×4×1 Monkhorst–Pack k-point mesh sampling for Brillouin-zone integration was used to optimize all surface structures52. To prevent interaction between two neighboring surfaces, the vacuum layer spacing was set to 15 Å. The transition state (TS) searches on CH4 activation process slab were carried out with the climbing-image nudged elastic band method (CI-NEB). All of the calculations were continued until the force has converged to less than 0.02 eV Å−1, and energies have converged within 10−5 eV. Data analysis and visualization were carried out by VASPKIT53 code and VESTA54. The ΔG of ECRR steps were calculated by:
ΔG = ΔEDFT + ΔEZPE - TΔS (8)

where ΔEDFT, ΔEZPE and ΔS were the energy from DFT optimization, correction of zero-point energy and the variation of entropy, respectively. T was the temperature (T = 298.15 K).

LOBSTER 4.1.0 package55 was employed for Crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) analysis to investigate local orbital interactions. This package works by projecting the plane-wave functions onto atomic orbital basis sets, thereby reconstructing the wave functions for specific local orbitals. Integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) was further calculated to provide a quantitative measure of the bonding strength and the orbital-specific contributions to chemical bonds56.

The AIMD simulations were performed using the CP2K package and the QUICKSTEP module57. For the investigation of the structural stability of Fe-Pd-N6C1 model, simulation temperature was set at 873.15 K using Nose–Hoover thermostat. AIMD simulation was lasted for 10 ps with a timestep of 1 fs. For the investigation of the activation of H2O2 and CH4, the simulation temperature was controlled at 335 K through a Nose–Hoover thermostat.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this study, the authors make an important conceptual contribution by proposing a novel mechanism of C-H bond activation using asymmetric charge distribution dual-sites. Firstly, the manuscript presents a novel strategy for incorporating the dual atomic Fe1-Pd1 sites within the periodical macropore (Fe1-Pd1 OMNC), which enables the efficient CH4 conversion under ambient conditions. The Fe1-Pd1 OMNC catalyst demonstrates exceptional photothermal catalytic performance, achieving a production rate of 16.2 mol gmetal-1 h-1 for C1 oxygenated products. Further mechanistic insights reveal that the asymmetric charge distribution on dual metal sites is able to stabilize the Hδ+ and CH3δ- fragments. This study represents a significant advancement given the systematic methodology and thorough theoretical investigation. Nevertheless, several specific issues require attention prior to publication, as outlined below:
1) The authors need to expand the discussion on the role of the macroporous skeleton in the photothermal catalytic CH4 conversion reaction.
2) The monodispersed PS template with a diameter of 270 nm was synthesized, but the aperture size of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC was measured as 200 nm (Fig. 1e). The authors are suggested to provide a proper explanation for the pore size shrinkage observed during the synthesis process.
3) The synthesized catalyst exhibits a regular tetradecahedral morphology, which appears to differ from the conventional dodecahedral structure of ZIF materials. The authors are recommended to add relevant discussion regarding this morphological distinction in the manuscript.
4) The authors mentioned in Fig. S16 the detection of formaldehyde products using a UV spectrophotometer, but the experimental methodology was not described. It is recommended to elaborate the analytical procedures in the Methods section.
5) The quantum efficiency of the photocatalytic system should be provided.
6) HCHO is a prevalent product that can be derived from the oxidation of CH3OH or the decomposition of CH3OOH. Can the authors explain why there is no HCHO produced in the methane oxidation reaction?
Minor point:
The authors are suggested to thoroughly check the format in the main text, supporting information and the figure axis labels.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Chen et al. developed a template-oriented encapsulation-pyrolysis protocol to integrate asymmetrically atomic sites on ordered macroporous N-doped carbon for photothermal catalytic selective oxidation of CH4. The catalysts were well characterized. The as-prepared Fe1-Pd1 OMNC demonstrates exceptional photothermal catalytic performance with high C1 oxygenate production rate with O2 serve as oxidant. The authors proposed a unique CH4 activation mechanism, in which a charge polarization region induced by the axial *O is able to break the first C-H bond, which is meaningful for the design of advanced catalytic system. This manuscript is well written with convincing experimental data. The findings are of great interest and may offer inspiring insights into the the in-depth understanding of heterogeneous interfacial catalysis. I recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications after minor revision.
1. In Figure 3c, the photothermal catalytic performance of the Fe1-Pd1 DOMNC is significantly lower than that of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC, highlighting the crucial role of the orderliness of macropores in photothermal catalytic systems. Thus, a detailed discussion is required.
2. It is recommended to supplement the error bars for the catalytic performance data in Figure 3.
3. Photocurrent response test is an effective mean to investigate the migration behavior of photo-induced carrier. So, it is suggested to supplement the relevant experimental data.
4. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and a brief analysis can be given to study the electrical properties of Fe1-Pd1 OMNC.
5. The selectivity of products should be mentioned in the abstract.
6. In Figure 5, it is recommended to provide the isosurface values of the differential density plots.
7. The reaction conditions of AIMD simulations should be provided in the caption.
8. It is recommended to mark the bonding and antibonding states in COHP.
9. The subscripts of H2O2/O2 on page 22 and the Zn (NO3)2·6(H2O) on page 23 should be corrected.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper reported a dual atomic Fe and Pd catalyst with periodic macroporous structure (Fe1-Pd1 OMNC) for photocatalytic CH4 conversion. Methane conversion has emerged as a topic of significant interest in recent years, driven by its dual implications for sustainable energy production and environmental mitigation. This manuscript addresses a relevant subject aligned with the journal’s scope and could generate broad interest among readers. However, due to the lack of sufficient innovation in the research and the experimental data presented fail to robustly substantiate the central claims, this manuscript cannot be recommended for publication in Nature Communications.
Critical concerns:
1. The primary innovation of this work lies in the activation of C-H bonds in CH4 via the charge-polarized region induced by on dual-single-atomic sites. However, the authors failed to identify the active sites and provide detailed mechanistic analysis and experimental validation of the C-H bond activation process. For example, the authors emphasize in the abstract and introduction that two mechanisms coexist during CH4 activation over Fe1-Pd1 OMNC: (1) electron transfer between the d orbitals of the catalyst and the σ orbitals of the C-H bond, leading to C-H bond cleavage, and (2) activation of the C-H bond through a local electrostatic field on the catalyst surface, inducing electrostatic CH3δ-–H δ+ polarization. While these mechanisms are individually similar to those reported in prior studies, the novelty of this work lies in their combined application. However, the results section does not explicitly demonstrate how these two mechanisms synergistically cooperate to activate the C-H bond in CH4.
2. Furthermore, the authors claim to manipulate C-H bond cleavage by engineering the electronic configuration of the catalyst surface. However, their proposed strategy of generating charge-polarized regions through charge transfer from Fe to active oxygen species to influence C-H bond polarization has already been reported (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 12357-12366). Furthermore, while they emphasize the impact of these charge-polarized regions and the role of orbital overlap on the reaction process, their conclusions rely solely on theoretical calculations and lack sufficient experimental validation, rendering the findings inadequately substantiated.
3. The experimental design for photocatalytic performance evaluation is not proper. For example, due to its high cost, H2O2 has been rarely selected as the oxidant in current catalytic systems, and its use typically does not involve pressurized conditions. Furthermore, the reported yield of methanol is predicated on minimal levels of the utilized catalyst (1-5 mg). It is a generally accepted principle that photocatalytic activity does not increase linearly with the mass of the catalyst. Given the minimal use of the catalyst, the quantity of methanol generated is, in comparison, relatively low.
4. Several critical data are notably absent from the manuscript. For example, quantum efficiency, carbon balance and CH4 conversion rate are all very important in evaluating the catalytic performance of CH4 conversion, but they are not given in this manuscript. The evaluation criteria for the products and the description of the product detection module are unclear. For example, it does not specify whether C2 products are detected and how a UV-visible spectrophotometer is used to measure HCHO. Additionally, key experiments should be repeated, and error bars should be included.
Other concerns:
1. The intensity ratio of the D band to the G band (ID/IG) in the Raman spectrum was not explicitly mentioned. This ratio needs to be supplemented to quantify the graphitization degree of the carbon matrix and to discuss its influence on the electron transport performance and the construction of the charge polarization region.

Generally, photo-derived heat and photoinduced electrons generated by a photothermal material

shows that the yield of C1 oxygenates decreases dramatically from 0.754 to 0.286 mmol h-1 when

purely photocatalytic system and the purely thermal catalysis is still less than that from the normal

effect between photogenerated electrons and photoinduced heat, beyond a simple additive effect.
As suggested, we subsequently measured the reaction rate at a constant temperature (i.e., 63 ℃)

overall reaction kinetics.

Upon reviewing the feedback, I note that the authors did not directly address the issue of orbital interaction raised in the previous comments, but instead opted for the removal of the related descriptions in the manuscript. Furthermore, although the authors have diligently addressed some of the reviewers' concerns, the following points require further attention.
1. The authors state that "heat and photoinduced electrons generated by Fe1-Pd1 OMNC under light irradiation would jointly participate in the oxidation of CH4, instead of undergoing a simple photo-derived thermal catalysis," but they do not explain the respective roles of photoinduced electrons and photogenerated heat in methane conversion, particularly regarding their effects on charge polarization. This requires the authors to provide additional experimental evidence for clarification.
2. The respective roles of photothermal heating and photoexcited charge carriers in driving the reaction are not definitively decoupled. The authors show that both pure thermal catalysis and pure photocatalysis (with cooling) yield lower activity than the photothermal condition. This correctly suggests a synergy but does not clarify the fundamental role of light beyond heating. Does the light primarily generate heat, which then drives a thermal catalytic cycle, or do photoexcited electrons directly participate in the catalytic steps (e.g., H2O2/O2 activation, C-H bond scission)? Measuring the reaction rate under identical temperature conditions while varying the light intensity (for a non- absorbing or weakly-absorbing catalyst at the excitation wavelength) could help distinguish between a purely thermal and a photo-assisted thermal process. This thereby proves the specific effect of the combined action of light and heat.
3. The synergy between Fe and Pd is demonstrated by comparing with single-atom catalysts. To rule out effects from simply having both metals present but not necessarily cooperating at an atomic level, could the authors prepare and test a physical mixture of Fe1 OMNC and Pd1 OMNC? This control would more conclusively prove that the synergy requires the proximate dual-atom sites.
4. Although the authors have conducted control experiments on the effect of light intensity on catalytic performance, the specific light intensity value that was selected has not been clearly stated. This parameter should be clearly reported in the experimental conditions for other control experiments.

After carefully evaluating the authors’ revisions and supplementary explanations in response to the review comments, it is considered that the main scientific issues in the original manuscript have been adequately addressed and resolved. However, some details should be noted. For example, the wavenumber (cm⁻¹) on the horizontal axis of the FTIR spectra in the text is currently arranged in ascending order. It is recommended to uniformly adjust it to the conventional display format of descending order (i.e., from high to low wavenumber). Therefore, acceptance after revision is recommended.
